source_refs.note: Chapter 22 exercise (PDF 98-100), solved: 10 MCQs keyed (no key is printed), 5 short-answer (with parts), 6 constructed-response and 4 descriptive questions with model answers. MCQ VIII, MCQ X and Q2 a, c, d carry Book corrections.

blocks.prompt: I. Which compound can be oxidised to form (CH₃)₂CHCOCH₃?
blocks.explanation: (CH₃)₂CHCOCH₃ is a ketone (3-methylbutan-2-one). Ketones come from the oxidation of secondary alcohols with the same skeleton: (CH₃)₂CH–CH(OH)–CH₃ (3-methylbutan-2-ol) + [O] → (CH₃)₂CH–CO–CH₃ + H₂O. (a) and (b) are primary (give aldehydes); (c) is tertiary (not oxidised).

blocks.prompt: II. Which alcohol forms a mixture of alkenes when dehydrated?
blocks.explanation: In pentan-2-ol, CH₃–CH(OH)–CH₂CH₂CH₃, the –OH carbon has two different β-carbons (C1 and C3) with hydrogens, so water can be removed in two ways: pent-1-ene and pent-2-ene. Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol give only propene; pentan-1-ol gives pent-1-ene.

blocks.prompt: III. Which alcohol can be oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate(VI) but cannot be dehydrated by heating with concentrated sulfuric acid?
blocks.explanation: 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol, (CH₃)₃C–CH₂OH, is a primary alcohol, so dichromate oxidises it. Its β-carbon is bonded to three CH₃ groups and has no hydrogen, so H₂O cannot be eliminated. (a) and (c) are tertiary (not oxidised); (d) is secondary and can be dehydrated.

blocks.prompt:
IV. Which one of the following mechanisms is not involved in the reaction sequence below?
CH₃CH₃ → CH₃CH₂Cl → CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂ = CH₂ → CH₃CH₂Br
blocks.explanation:
CH₃CH₃ → CH₃CH₂Cl: free-radical substitution (Cl₂, light).
CH₃CH₂Cl → CH₃CH₂OH: nucleophilic substitution (aqueous NaOH).
CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂: elimination (dehydration).
CH₂=CH₂ → CH₃CH₂Br: electrophilic addition of HBr.
Electrophilic substitution (a reaction of arenes) does not occur.

blocks.prompt: V. Which one of the following does not represent an oxidation?
blocks.explanation: Ethanal → ethanol is a reduction (addition of hydrogen, e.g. by NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄): CH₃CHO + 2[H] → CH₃CH₂OH. The other three are oxidations of alcohols (1° → aldehyde, 2° → ketone, 1° → carboxylic acid).

blocks.prompt: VI. Dehydration of alcohol is an example of
blocks.explanation: Dehydration is an elimination reaction in which a water molecule (H from the β-carbon and –OH) is removed to form an alkene: CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O.

blocks.prompt: VII. Bromine reacts with phenol and decolourise orange color and turns it to which of the colored precipitate?
blocks.explanation: Phenol decolourises orange bromine water at room temperature and gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol: C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr.

blocks.prompt: VIII. When phenol is treated with excess bromine water it gives m-bromophenol?
blocks.explanation: The –OH group activates the ring and directs the electrophile to the 2, 4 and 6 positions. With excess bromine water all three are substituted: C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white ppt) + 3HBr. m-Bromophenol is not formed.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question is misprinted: it ends “it gives m-bromophenol?” as if asking a yes/no question, and only three options (a–c) are printed. It should ask what phenol gives with excess bromine water; the answer is 2,4,6-tribromophenol, not m-bromophenol.

blocks.prompt:
IX. What are the correct reagents for the conversion below?
CH₃CH₂CHOHCH₃ → CH₃CH₂CHBrCH₃
blocks.explanation:
The –OH is replaced by Br. NaBr (like KBr) with H₂SO₄ gives HBr in the flask, which converts the alcohol into the bromoalkane:
CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ + NaBr + H₂SO₄ → CH₃CH₂CHBrCH₃ + NaHSO₄ + H₂O

blocks.prompt: X. Give a chemical test used in distinguishing propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol.
blocks.explanation: Propan-2-ol has the CH₃–CH(OH)– group, so with a halogen and NaOH it is oxidised to propanone and gives the haloform reaction; propan-1-ol does not. This is the intended answer. Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ turns green with both (both are oxidised), SOCl₂ converts both to chloroalkanes, and NaOH(aq) reacts with neither. See the Book correction.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The usual test is the iodoform test with I₂ and NaOH (taught in Chapter 23): propan-2-ol gives a yellow precipitate of tri-iodomethane (CHI₃), propan-1-ol gives none. With Br₂ and NaOH the product is bromoform, a liquid, so no clear precipitate is seen. Option (a) is keyed as the intended answer; it should read “I₂ and NaOH”.

blocks.prompt:
a) Six alcohols are given below:
i. butan-2-ol  ii. ethane-1,2-diol  iii. 2-methylpentan-3-ol  iv. 2-methylpropan-2-ol  v. propan-1-ol  vi. propan-2-ol
i) Which alcohol is an example of a tertiary alcohol?
ii) Which alcohol is an example of an alcohol that can be oxidized to carboxylic acid?.
iii) Which alcohol is an example of an alcohol that can be oxidized to a ketone?
v) Which alcohol can't change color of acidified potassium dichromate?
blocks.explanation:
i) iv. 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH (OH carbon joined to three carbons).
ii) v. propan-1-ol (primary): CH₃CH₂CH₂OH → [O] propanal → [O] propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH.
iii) A secondary alcohol: vi. propan-2-ol → propanone (also i. butan-2-ol and iii. 2-methylpentan-3-ol).
v) iv. 2-methylpropan-2-ol: a tertiary alcohol is not oxidised, so the orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ stays orange.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The parts of Q2(a) are numbered i), ii), iii), v): part iv) is missing from the numbering (no question is lost).

blocks.prompt:
b) Phenylamine reacts with HNO₂(aq) at 4°C to form compound P. Compound P reacts with phenol under alkaline conditions at 4°C. The product of this reaction is acidified, forming azo compound Q.
i) Draw the structure of compound P and Q.
ii) Circle the azo group on your structure.
iii) State one use of an azo compound such as Q.
blocks.explanation:
i) P = benzenediazonium chloride, C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻: a benzene ring bonded to –N⁺≡N (diazonium group), with Cl⁻.
C₆H₅NH₂ + HNO₂ + HCl → C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + 2H₂O (below 10 °C)
Q = 4-hydroxyazobenzene, C₆H₅–N=N–C₆H₄–OH: a benzene ring joined through –N=N– to a second ring that carries –OH at the para (4) position.
C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + C₆H₅OH → C₆H₅–N=N–C₆H₄OH + HCl
ii) The azo group is the –N=N– linking the two rings.
iii) Azo compounds are coloured and are used as dyes (azo dyes); the –N=N– group is the chromophore.

blocks.prompt:
c) Cyclohexane can be converted into cyclohexene via a three stage synthesis.
(Scheme: cyclohexane → stage 1, Cl₂ → compound A → stage 2 → cyclohexanol → stage 3 → cyclohexene.)
i) In stage 1, cyclohexane reacts with chlorine to form the organic product, compound A. Show the structure of compound A.
ii) Stage 3 involves the dehydration of an alcohol. State a suitable reagent for dehydrating an alcohol.
iii) Write a balanced equation for the dehydration of cyclohexanol, C₆H₁₁OH.
blocks.explanation:
i) A = chlorocyclohexane, C₆H₁₁Cl: a ring of six carbons (five CH₂ and one CH) with Cl on the CH carbon. C₆H₁₂ + Cl₂ → (light) C₆H₁₁Cl + HCl (free-radical substitution). Stage 2: heat A with aqueous NaOH → cyclohexanol.
ii) Concentrated H₂SO₄ (or concentrated H₃PO₄, or heated Al₂O₃).
iii) C₆H₁₁OH → (conc. H₂SO₄, heat) C₆H₁₀ + H₂O

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the printed scheme cyclohexanol is labelled “cyclohexannol” (misspelt), and stage 1 shows only Cl₂; chlorination of an alkane also needs light (UV).

d) There are four structurally isomeric alcohols of molecular formula C₄H₁₀O. Graphical formulae of these isomers, labelled A, B, C and D, are shown below.
(As printed: A = CH₃–C(CH₃)₂–OH; B = CH₃–CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–OH; C = CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–OH; D = CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–OH.)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Structure B is printed with five carbons, CH₃–CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–OH (2-methylbutan-2-ol, C₅H₁₂O), so it is not an isomer of C₄H₁₀O. The fourth C₄H₁₀O alcohol is butan-2-ol, CH₃–CH(OH)–CH₂–CH₃ (secondary), which was probably meant. Answers below give both readings.

blocks.prompt: i) Identify the type of alcohol represented by A and by B.
blocks.explanation: A is a tertiary alcohol: the C–OH carbon is joined to three carbons. B as printed is also tertiary (C–OH joined to three carbons); if B is butan-2-ol (the intended C₄H₁₀O isomer), it is secondary.

blocks.prompt: ii) Give the name of alcohol A.
blocks.explanation: A, (CH₃)₃C–OH, is 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

blocks.prompt: iii) Select one of the alcohols A, B, C or D which will, on oxidation, produce an aldehyde. Give the structural formula of the aldehyde produced by this reaction.
blocks.explanation:
C (butan-1-ol), a primary alcohol: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO (butanal) + H₂O.
(D, also primary, gives 2-methylpropanal, (CH₃)₂CH–CHO.)

blocks.prompt: iv) All the alcohols A, B, C and D may be readily dehydrated. Explain what is meant by the term dehydration. State the type of compound formed by dehydration of alcohols.
blocks.explanation: Dehydration is an elimination reaction in which a molecule of water (–OH and an H from the neighbouring β-carbon) is removed from the alcohol. It forms an alkene, e.g. CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O.

blocks.prompt: v) Suggest suitable reagent(s) and condition(s) for the dehydration of alcohols.
blocks.explanation: Heat the alcohol with excess concentrated H₂SO₄ or concentrated H₃PO₄, or pass the alcohol vapour over heated aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃).

blocks.prompt: e) Select one of the alcohols A, B, C or D which, on dehydration, would give a single product. Draw the structural formula of this product.
blocks.explanation:
A, 2-methylpropan-2-ol: all three β-carbons are identical CH₃ groups, so only one alkene forms:
(CH₃)₃C–OH → CH₂=C(CH₃)₂ (2-methylpropene) + H₂O
Structure: a C=C double bond; one carbon carries two H atoms, the other carries two CH₃ groups. (D also gives only 2-methylpropene. B as printed, or butan-2-ol, has two different β-carbons and gives a mixture.)

blocks.prompt: I. Why nitration of phenol is easier than benzene. Which product is formed when phenol is nitrated with conc. HNO₃ at room temperature?
blocks.explanation:
One lone pair of the –OH oxygen is delocalised into the benzene ring, increasing its electron density; the ring is activated, so the electrophile NO₂⁺ attacks easily under mild conditions (dilute HNO₃, room temperature), at the 2, 4 and 6 positions. Benzene needs conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄ at 25–60 °C.
With conc. HNO₃: 2,4,6-trinitrophenol. C₆H₅OH + 3HNO₃ → C₆H₂(NO₂)₃OH + 3H₂O

blocks.prompt: ii. Sodium hydroxide reacts with phenol but not with ethanol. Give reason.
blocks.explanation: Phenol is a stronger acid (stronger than water): its phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of the negative charge into the ring, so it gives up H⁺ to OH⁻: C₆H₅OH + NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + H₂O. Ethanol is a weaker acid than water; the electron-donating ethyl group (+I) destabilises the ethoxide ion, so OH⁻ cannot remove its proton.

blocks.prompt: iii. Give reactions of methanol with SOCl₂, and PCl₅.
blocks.explanation:
CH₃OH + SOCl₂ → (pyridine) CH₃Cl + SO₂ + HCl
CH₃OH + PCl₅ → CH₃Cl + POCl₃ + HCl
In both, –OH is replaced by Cl to give chloromethane.

blocks.prompt: iv. How propanol can be converted into propanal?
blocks.explanation:
Oxidise propan-1-ol (a primary alcohol) with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇; orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ turns green Cr³⁺:
CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + [O] → (H⁺/K₂Cr₂O₇) CH₃CH₂CHO + H₂O
The aldehyde is distilled off as it forms so that it is not oxidised further to propanoic acid (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: v. Write down the reaction for the substitution of each of Cl, Br, and I with –OH in 2-propanol.
blocks.explanation:
Cl: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + HCl → (ZnCl₂) CH₃CHClCH₃ + H₂O
Br: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + KBr + H₂SO₄ → CH₃CHBrCH₃ + KHSO₄ + H₂O
I: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + KI + H₃PO₄ → CH₃CHICH₃ + KH₂PO₄ + H₂O
(H₃PO₄ is used for iodoalkanes because it is a weak oxidizing agent and does not oxidize I⁻ to I₂.)

blocks.prompt: vi. Construct a reaction for the preparation of nitro-substituted naphthol. Is there produced a single product? Explain.
blocks.explanation:
1-naphthol + dilute HNO₃ (room temperature) → 2-nitro-1-naphthol + 4-nitro-1-naphthol + H₂O
C₁₀H₇OH + HNO₃ → C₁₀H₆(NO₂)OH + H₂O
No, a mixture forms: the –OH group activates the naphthalene ring and directs the electrophile to both the 2 and 4 positions (9 and 10 carry no H).

blocks.prompt: Q4. Explain the acidity of phenol
blocks.explanation:
Phenol, C₆H₅OH, is weakly acidic: in water it partly loses a proton from its –OH group.
C₆H₅OH(aq) ⇌ C₆H₅O⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq)
Reason: one of the lone pairs on the oxygen of the phenoxide ion overlaps with the delocalised π system of the benzene ring. The negative charge is therefore spread over the ring (to the 2, 4 and 6 carbons) instead of staying on oxygen. This delocalisation stabilises the phenoxide ion, the conjugate base. With less charge density on oxygen, H⁺ is not strongly attracted back, so phenol is more likely to lose a proton (act as an acid) than to gain one.
Comparison: in an alcohol the alkyl group is electron donating (+I effect); it pushes electron density onto the oxygen of the alkoxide ion and destabilises it, so alcohols ionise less than water. Relative acidity: phenol > water > ethanol.
Evidence:
1. Phenol dissolves in NaOH to form a salt and water (ethanol does not): C₆H₅OH + NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + H₂O
2. Molten phenol reacts vigorously with sodium, giving H₂: 2C₆H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₆H₅ONa + H₂
Phenol is only slightly soluble in water because of its large non-polar benzene ring, but it dissolves in alkaline solutions as the soluble phenoxide salt.

blocks.prompt: Q5. Explain why the reagents and conditions for the nitration and bromination of phenol are different from those for benzene.
blocks.explanation:
In phenol the –OH group is attached to the benzene ring. One lone pair of the oxygen overlaps with the π system of the ring and becomes delocalised, so the electron density of the ring increases. The ring is activated and is attacked by electrophiles much more easily than benzene; the –OH group directs the electrophile to the 2, 4 and 6 positions. Therefore milder reagents are enough, and substitution often goes to all three positions.
Nitration:
Benzene: conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄, refluxed at 25–60 °C → nitrobenzene.
Phenol: dilute HNO₃ at room temperature → 2-nitrophenol + 4-nitrophenol; with conc. HNO₃ → 2,4,6-trinitrophenol.
Bromination:
Benzene: pure bromine (not a solution) with anhydrous AlBr₃ catalyst at room temperature → bromobenzene.
Phenol: bromine water, no catalyst, room temperature; the orange colour disappears and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol forms: C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr.

rows: Ring activated by the –OH lone pair (more electron density)
Nitration: dilute HNO₃ at room temperature
Nitration: conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄, reflux 25–60 °C
Bromination: bromine water, no catalyst, room temperature
Bromination: pure Br₂ with anhydrous AlBr₃ catalyst

blocks.prompt: Q6. Describe how phenylamine can be converted into phenol, including reagents and conditions.
blocks.explanation:
The conversion takes place in three steps through a diazonium salt.
Step 1 (nitrous acid in situ): HNO₂ is unstable, so it is made in the test tube from sodium nitrite and dilute hydrochloric acid, kept below 10 °C with ice:
NaNO₂ + HCl → HNO₂ + NaCl
Step 2 (diazotisation, below 10 °C): phenylamine reacts with HNO₂ and HCl to form benzenediazonium chloride:
C₆H₅NH₂ + HNO₂ + HCl → C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + 2H₂O
The low temperature is needed because the diazonium salt is unstable and decomposes, giving off N₂, even at room temperature.
Step 3 (hydrolysis): the diazonium salt solution is warmed with water; nitrogen gas is evolved and phenol is formed:
C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + H₂O → (warm) C₆H₅OH + N₂ + HCl

blocks.prompt: Q7. Explain why ethanol is less acidic than water, but water is less acidic than phenol.
blocks.explanation:
Acidity depends on how easily H⁺ is lost, i.e. on how stable the ion left behind (the conjugate base) is.
CH₃CH₂OH ⇌ CH₃CH₂O⁻ + H⁺   H₂O ⇌ OH⁻ + H⁺   C₆H₅OH ⇌ C₆H₅O⁻ + H⁺
Ethanol < water: the ethyl group is electron donating (positive inductive effect, +I). It pushes electron density onto the oxygen of the ethoxide ion, so the negative charge is more concentrated and the ion is destabilised. CH₃CH₂O⁻ readily accepts H⁺ again to re-form ethanol, so ethanol has a lower [H⁺] than water. Evidence: sodium reacts with ethanol less vigorously than with water (with phenolphthalein, pink appears slowly with ethanol, at once with water).
Water < phenol: in the phenoxide ion one lone pair of oxygen overlaps with the delocalised π system of the benzene ring, so the negative charge is spread over the ring. This stabilises C₆H₅O⁻ and lowers the charge density on oxygen, so H⁺ is not strongly attracted back. Phenol therefore loses H⁺ more easily than water; it even reacts with NaOH: C₆H₅OH + NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + H₂O.
Order of acidity: phenol > water > ethanol.
